demand_description: Athlete throws the cross into a stationary hand target (coach's palm), at half speed, with the coach's other hand resting lightly on the athlete's lead glove/cheekbone throughout the punch and return. The tactile contact gives instant feedback the moment the lead hand drifts, so the athlete feels correct hand position rather than guessing at it. Slow speed removes timing pressure entirely — the only job is cross, feel the lead hand stay home, return.

demand_description: Same cross-and-return, but the coach calls the cross on a random verbal or visual cue while the athlete is already shuffling/circling, and immediately on return flicks a soft, telegraphed jab at the exact spot the lead hand should be covering. If the lead hand was down, the flick lands; if it held its position, it doesn't — the check becomes self-scoring instead of coach-called. Unpredictable timing and footwork disruption add decision load before the punch, and the incoming flick adds consequence after it, but the lesson stays identical: lead hand discipline through the throw and the recovery.

demand_description: Partner throws a pre-announced sequence of the same three punches every time (jab–cross–hook), and the athlete pre-selects the matching defense for each (slip the jab, parry the cross, catch the hook) before the attacks start. This removes the read-and-choose demand under uncertainty while still requiring the athlete to physically string three *different* defensive tools together in order — the layering behaviour stays intact, just with the decision pre-made. Contact stays conditioned; only the punch order and defense selection are fixed and known.

demand_description: Partner attacks freely, can repeat a punch type back-to-back or feint, and is allowed to close angle or step laterally between attacks, forcing the athlete to recognize repetition/false starts and still avoid using the same defensive response twice in a row. A second stressor: the coach calls out a "banned" defense mid-exchange (e.g., "no slipping"), removing the athlete's default option and forcing a live substitution. The rule under test doesn't change — different defense each time, no spamming one tool — the drill just removes predictability so the athlete has to generate that variety under recognition pressure rather than a known pattern.
coach_watch_point: Does the harder version still display the same lesson, or has it changed the problem entirely.

The picture is simplified to "hear name, throw known combo" — the athlete gets clean, repeatable hits on recognizing and firing the called sequence without any guessing about timing or which combo is coming.
